stories.title: Bid to restore rare Atlantic rainforest secures £6m lottery grant
summary: Hubs offering training in conservation work are to be set up in Torridon, Morvern and mid-Argyll.

stories.title: Artist creates world's biggest soil painting
summary: Phil Lambert used four types of soil, including some collected from his mother, to create his work.

stories.title: Scientists discover why some mosquitoes love you and others don't
summary: A surprising new study reveals that mosquitoes have very different tastes in humans, with each species attracted to its own combination of skin odors, chemicals, and bacteria.
The discovery challenges the idea of a universal mosquito magnet and could lead to more effective repellents against dangerous disease-spreading mosquitoes.

stories.title: Scientists discover a giant 66-pound rodent that lived 34 million years ago
summary: Scientists have uncovered fossils of a giant rodent that lived in Thailand 34 million years ago, revealing that enormous rodents evolved much earlier than previously thought.
Named Yakamys sirindhornae, the ancient animal may have weighed around 66 pounds, roughly twice as much as other known rodents of its time.

stories.title: 237-million-year-old fossils reveal a bizarre armored sea amphibian
summary: A bizarre, heavily armored amphibian roamed the oceans 237 million years ago, despite the fact that modern amphibians cannot survive entirely in saltwater.
Discovered in China, the giant salamander-sized creature may be the first known amphibian to have adapted to a fully marine existence.

stories.title: Duchy tenants may have to buy farms or leave as Prince William plans sell-off
summary: A ten-year strategy to raise £500m from the Duchy of Cornwall will see farms sold off across England.

stories.title: Astronomers discover hidden alien planet in James Webb images
summary: A breakthrough in telescope imaging could reveal countless alien worlds that have been hiding in plain sight.

Scientists developed a new technique that uses a digital twin of the James Webb Space Telescope to remove the overwhelming glare of stars, making faint exoplanets two to 15 times easier to detect than with conventional methods.
The technology has already uncovered a previously hidden planet in existing telescope data and could reveal many more.

stories.title: A mysterious 93-billion-mile cosmic structure may be the wreckage of colliding worlds
summary: NASA's Hubble Space Telescope has revealed surprising new details about a mysterious, 93-billion-mile-long cloud of dark, fluffy dust that may have formed when massive planetary bodies collided.
The discovery challenges previous assumptions about the structure and offers new clues about the violent birth of planetary systems.

stories.title: Paleontologists discover “one-in-a-million” fossil with 450-million-year-old soft tissue
summary: Scientists have discovered a remarkably preserved 450-million-year-old fossil containing soft tissues from an ancient starfish relative, revealing unexpected details about marine life more than 200 million years before dinosaurs existed.
Found in a museum collection, the extraordinarily rare specimen offers new clues about how Earth's earliest reef animals fed, survived, and evolved.

stories.title: Comets may have destroyed life's ingredients instead of delivering them to Earth
summary: A century-old theory about the origins of life on Earth may be wrong.

New research from the University of Cambridge suggests that comets traveled too fast and struck at unfavorable angles for the fragile molecules needed for life to survive, making successful delivery extraordinarily unlikely.
The findings point toward asteroids or chemical processes on Earth as more plausible sources of life's building blocks.

stories.title: Locals launch campaign to buy ancient wood
summary: Locals have a year to raise the money needed to buy Ruscombe Wood near Stroud.

stories.title: House martin artificial nests scheme set to expand
summary: The artificial nests are more robust than the endangered migratory birds' own mud creations.

stories.title: The swan sanctuary wetland fighting climate change
summary: The global campaign to restore the "soggy secret weapon" that can combat against climate change.

stories.title: NASA’s CHAPEA Mars crew finally emerges after more than a year in isolation
summary: After more than a year of simulated life on Mars, four NASA volunteers have finally emerged from isolation, bringing a remarkable space exploration experiment to an end.
Their experiences growing food, conserving resources, and overcoming Mars-like challenges could help NASA prepare for humanity's future on the Moon and Mars.

stories.title: Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low
summary: Even when bad cholesterol is brought down to healthy levels, some people remain at risk of heart attacks, and scientists may have discovered why.
Researchers identified two types of fat-carrying particles that appear to promote inflammation and damage blood vessels through mechanisms beyond cholesterol buildup.

stories.title: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain
summary: A surprising discovery suggests that some early signs of Alzheimer’s disease may begin outside the brain.

Using miniature laboratory systems made from human cells, scientists found that genetic mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s can disrupt nerve-to-muscle connections without any involvement from the brain or spinal cord.
This could help explain why some patients experience changes in balance, walking, and coordination long before memory problems develop.

stories.title: After 40 years, CERN finds evidence of a one-in-10-billion particle decay
summary: CERN scientists have finally found evidence of a particle decay so rare that it happens only once in roughly 10 billion decays, ending a search spanning more than 40 years.
The breakthrough could help physicists uncover hidden particles and forces that lie beyond the reach of today's most powerful accelerators.

stories.title: Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee
summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden gut-to-brain dopamine pathway that helps explain why bitter coffee and other initially unpleasant flavors can become favorites over time.
The discovery reveals how the brain learns to crave certain foods and could eventually lead to new ways of reshaping eating habits and food preferences.
